title: AUTOMATION OF VISUAL INSPECTION USING IMAGE PROCESSING

items.abstract: <jats:p>Industrial surface-inspection systems usually return anomaly scores, classification labels, or segmentation masks, but operators often need direct answers to repeated visual questions: whether a defect is present, what morphology is visible, where it appears, how large its visible extent is, and whether the case should be reviewed. General vision-language models can express such answers, but their compute cost and weak grounding are poorly matched to a fixed-camera edge station. This paper presents Tiny Defect-VQA, a bounded visual question answering system for industrial image interpretation under explicit latency and memory limits. The data engine converts published defect labels and pixel masks into image-disjoint question-answer records using a versioned inspection ontology. The model combines a MobileNetV3-Small visual encoder, a compact two-layer question encoder, mask-guided question pooling, and low-rank gated fusion to predict both a typed answer and a defect heatmap. Post-hoc temperature scaling and question-specific thresholds route uncertain predictions to manual review. Under a locked five-seed protocol, Tiny Defect-VQA achieves 89.6% mean answer accuracy, 87.8% macro-F1, and 61.3% mask IoU, improving over the best matched compact baseline by 5.1 percentage points in accuracy and 5.7 points in macro-F1. Question-specific abstention reduces selective risk to 2.7% at 80% automatic-answer coverage. End-to-end Jetson Nano profiling reports 28.4 ms median latency and 431 MB peak memory, satisfying the declared 50-ms and 512-MB edge limits. These results position Tiny Defect-VQA as a quantitative, mask-grounded interface for real-world edge surface inspection.</jats:p>
title: Tiny Defect-VQA: Mask-Grounded Edge Visual Question Answering for Industrial Surface Inspection

items.abstract: <jats:p>Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) can improve question answering with large language models by anchoring model-generated answers on retrieved evidence. Nevertheless, the RAG systems are prone to generating an answer even when the retrieved evidence is lacking. It raises a question about the reliability of such approach in biomedical question answering, where unreliable response reduces the trustworthiness of the generated answers. This paper aims at investigating whether the use of retrieval confidence and evidence verification can enable reliable selective abstention of the biomedical RAG system. The experiment employs a labeled subset of PubMedQA containing 1,000 biomedical questions. A stratified validation set consisted of 200 questions and a held-out test set contained 800 questions. A RAG pipeline includes the following steps: dense retrieval, hybrid dense-BM25 retrieval, cross-encoder reranking, FLAN-T5-based answer generation, and Natural Language Inference (NLI)-based evidence verification. To examine how the system behaves when there is no sufficient evidence, a controlled stress test was designed by stripping away gold-associated retrieved passages from the retrieved context before answer generation in a random subset of questions. The reliability score calculated using normalized retrieval confidence and evidence-verification probability was calibrated based on the validation set and decided the system's decision to abstain from answering. The reliability mechanism calibration identified a retrieval weight of 0.90, an evidence-verification weight of 0.10, and an abstention threshold of 0.35. On the held-out test set of 800 questions out of which 146 are designed to have insufficient evidence, the technique scored 89.62% abstention precision, 65.07% recall, and 75.40% F1 while maintaining 86.75% coverage. The model correctly identified 95 insufficient evidence cases but abstained from answering 11 other questions (false positives). The change in selective answering improved the accuracy of answers by 0.23% points, from 53.37% to 53.60%. Thus, the results demonstrate that a well-calibrated reliability signal is able to detect a number of cases with insufficient evidence with a high degree of precision and preserve coverage of the majority of question answering. However, the approach did not provide any significant improvement of the answer generation model accuracy.</jats:p>
title: Evaluating Evidence Verification and Selective Abstention for Reliable Retrieval-Augmented Biomedical Question Answering

items.abstract: <jats:p>The fact that you are reading this article indicates that you have optical sensors (eyes). Pick up a pencil from your desk. You will almost certainly locate it visually, guiding your hand towards it by employing visual feedback. Is the tip of the pencil broken? Again, you will probably use optical rather than, say tactile or functional‐testing methods. Over the aeons of our evolutionary history, nature has found that remote sensing by vision is a most valuable facility. It is fast, safer than tactile sensing and can operate over considerable distances. It seems eminently sensible to consider whether these lessons that we learn from nature can be applied in the workshop.</jats:p>

items.abstract: <jats:p>If two elections are held at the same day, why do some people choose to vote in one but to abstain in another? We argue that selective abstention is driven by same factors that determine voter turnout. Our empirical analysis focuses on Sweden where the turnout gap between local and national elections has been about 2-3%. Rich administrative registry data reveal that people from higher socio-economic backgrounds, immigrants, women, older individuals, and people who have been less geographically mobile are less likely to selectively abstain.</jats:p>

title: Intelligent visual inspection

items.abstract:
<jats:p>In industrial manufacturing, ensuring quality control is critical to maintaining high standards and operational efficiency. Manual defect detection, however, is often time-consuming, error-prone, and costly, thereby driving the need for automated solutions. This paper investigates a technique for industrial anomaly detection (IAD) by utilizing the state-of-the-art PatchCore algorithm in conjunction with the widely recognized MVTec AD dataset. The dataset consists of 5354 high-resolution color images representing diverse objects and textures, including defect-free samples for training and numerous anomalous instances for testing. With over seventy distinct defect types—such as scratches, dents, contamination, and other structural irregularities—the dataset presents substantial challenges for conventional visual inspection (VI) techniques. The approach integrates convolutional neural networks (CNNs) with patch-based feature extraction methods, enabling PatchCore to accurately identify and localize even subtle anomalies within complex industrial imagery. Experimental results demonstrate that PatchCore significantly enhances detection accuracy, reduces false positives, and streamlines the overall inspection process. These improvements have important implications for operational productivity and quality assurance in various industrial sectors, paving the way for more reliable and cost-effective manufacturing practices.
 

 
Received: 31 May 2025 | Revised: 26 September 2025 | Accepted: 22 December 2025
 
Conflicts of Interest
The authors declare that they have no conflicts of interest to this work.
 
Data Availability Statement
The data that support the findings of this study are openly available at https://www.mvtec.com/company/research/datasets/mvtec-ad.

Shalini Kumari: Conceptualization, Software, analysis, Resources, Data curation, Writing – original draft. Chander Prabha: Methodology, Validation, Investigation, Writing – review & editing, Visualization, Supervision, Project administration.</jats:p>

items.abstract: <jats:p>This article has the specific objectives of highlighting the computer vision techniques used in the IVAP project, discussing the stages of implementation of the system and analyzing the results obtained. Throughout this study, we hope to contribute to the existing literature on the application of computer vision in industry, citing examples from authors such as Gerald J. Agin (1980) and Rodrigo Barbosa Davies (2012), who explored the practice and effectiveness of these technologies in industrial settings. Computer vision has established itself as an essential tool for visual inspection in industrial production lines, promoting significant improvements in the quality and efficiency of manufacturing processes. This study addresses the implementation of an advanced computer vision system in the IVAP (Visual Autonomous Product Inspection) project, developed in partnership between the Conecthus Institute and Vantiva. The implementation of the Keyence CV-X Series system was motivated by the need to perform autonomous inspections, standardizing product quality without relying on manual evaluations, which are prone to errors. The development of the project focused on the use of sophisticated computer vision techniques, including defect detection and classification through machine learning algorithms for image processing and cosmetic defect analysis. The techniques used were studied and adapted to the industrial context, allowing the detailed inspection of cosmetic aspects of the products, with minimal exceptions. These techniques, which included lighting adjustments, camera sensitivity, and algorithms for detecting smudges and scratches, were crucial to the system's effectiveness. </jats:p>
